newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poehl opposes dogmatic interpretation of Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: Poehl opposes dogmatic interpretation of Maastricht.

text.p: Former German Bundesbank head Karl Otto Poehl said on Sunday that terms for European monetary union should not be interpreted dogmatically -- or else Germany might not qualify for the single currency's launch in 1999.

Poehl, speaking on Hesse radio, said he did not expect Germany to meet all the criteria set in the Maastricht treaty next year -- when fitness for taking part in the issue of the single currency will be judged.
But, he added, politicians would find a way of expressing the criteria so that Germany can meet them "because if the currency does not come in 1999, it may never come at all."

Poehl was joining a debate in Germany about whether the Maastricht terms should be strictly enforced. Interpretation could decide whether it is based on a core of European Union states or includes countries from the so-called periphery.
Current Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer has spoken out for a strict interpretation of Maastricht, as have government leaders in Bonn.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking in Washington on Saturday, praised G7 partner Italy for proposing an austere 1997 budget putting it into the frame for EMU membership.

Poehl said the limits on new government borrowing of at or near three percent of gross domestic product and of total state debt of 60 percent of GDP were "purely coincidental" and should not become a dogma.

He also described the single currency as an experiment with an unknown outcome, and warned of possible disagreement between Germany and France due to differing policy approaches. Germany, Poehl said, targets maintaining the value of money while France makes the exchange rate its top priority.
The common currency is unlikely to create new jobs, and could even cause higher unemployment in less competitive countries, Poehl warned.
